ownership.what: Rust's core memory safety feature - each value has ONE owner
rules: Each value has exactly one owner
When the owner goes out of scope, the value is dropped (freed)
You can transfer ownership (move) or lend it (borrow)

example_move.code:
let s1 = String::from("hello");
let s2 = s1; // s1 is MOVED to s2, can't use s1 anymore
example_move.explanation: s1 no longer valid after this line

example_clone.code:
let s1 = String::from("hello");
let s2 = s1.clone(); // Both s1 and s2 are valid
example_clone.explanation: Make a copy when you need both

borrowing.what: Temporarily lending data without transferring ownership

immutable_borrow.rule: Can have MANY immutable borrows at once

mutable_borrow.rule: Can have ONLY ONE mutable borrow at a time
mutable_borrow.why: Prevents data races - can't modify while someone else is reading

common_mistake.explanation: Mutable borrows can't overlap - use scopes to separate them

mut_keyword.make_it_mutable: let mut x = 5; x = 10; // Now you can change it
when_to_use: Use `mut` when the variable will change
Use `&mut` when a function needs to modify borrowed data

examples.variable:
let mut list = List::New();
list.Add(42); // Need mut to modify
examples.dont_need: let name = String::from("Alice"); // Don't need mut if never changing

lifetimes.what: Tell Rust how long borrowed data lives
lifetimes.when_needed: Only when compiler can't figure it out (usually with multiple references)
lifetimes.syntax: 'a is a lifetime name (like a generic, but for lifetimes)

example_simple.explanation: The returned reference lives as long as 'items' does

example_complex.explanation: Output lives as long as BOTH inputs (whichever is shorter)

common_dixscript_case.scenario: Token stores references to source code
common_dixscript_case.solution: Either copy the data (String) or use lifetimes if storing references (&str)

when_not_needed: Single input reference → Output lifetime is obvious
Using owned types (String, Vec, etc.) instead of references

ignore_param.explanation: The underscore _ means 'I don't care about this value'
ignore_param.use_case: When Match requires a function but you don't need the error: |_| panic!("Unexpected error")

c_sharp_comparison.rust: return Ok(42); // Type inference knows it's Result<i32, DixError>

str.always_borrowed: &str (never own a str, only borrow it)

when_porting.why: &str is more flexible - accepts both owned and borrowed strings

step_by_step_porting.2_identify_dependencies: What other types does it use?
step_by_step_porting.3_check_skills: Is there a skill for this? (e.g., /mnt/skills/public/...)
step_by_step_porting.5_port_struct: Convert C# class to Rust struct
step_by_step_porting.8_fix_types: String vs &str, Vec vs slice, etc.

cannot_move_out_of_borrowed_content.error: cannot move out of `*list` which is behind a shared reference
cannot_move_out_of_borrowed_content.cause: Trying to take ownership of borrowed data
cannot_move_out_of_borrowed_content.fix: Use .clone() if you need ownership: let owned = borrowed.clone();

cannot_borrow_as_mutable.error: cannot borrow `x` as mutable more than once
cannot_borrow_as_mutable.cause: Two mutable borrows at same time
cannot_borrow_as_mutable.fix: Use scopes: { let r1 = &mut x; } let r2 = &mut x;

temporary_value_dropped.fix: Store the value in a variable first: let temp = create_value(); let ref_to_temp = &temp;

expected_reference_found_type.cause: Type mismatch between owned and borrowed
expected_reference_found_type.fix: Use &string or string.as_str() to convert String to &str

when_stuck: 1. Read the compiler error CAREFULLY - Rust errors are helpful
2. Search docs.rs for the type causing issues
4. Check if there's a Rust equivalent: 'C# List to Rust equivalent'
5. Ask for help - explain what you're trying to do
debugging: Use dbg!(value); to print and return value
Use the logger for structured output
performance: Use &str instead of String when possible
Use iterators instead of collecting to Vec
testing: Write tests BEFORE porting complex functions
Test incrementally - don't wait until everything is done

immediate: 4. Write tests for each function as you port
